subject: History
topic: British Governors-General and Viceroys of India — mixed tiers
description: Warren Hastings to Mountbatten, key reforms / events under each

questions.stem: The FIRST Governor-General of British India (Bengal Presidency) was:

options.option_text: Lord Cornwallis, who later codified land revenue
Warren Hastings, appointed under the 1773 Regulating Act
Lord Wellesley, who started subsidiary alliances
Lord Dalhousie, of Doctrine of Lapse fame

questions.explanation: Warren Hastings (1772-1785) — first Governor-General of Bengal, appointed under the Regulating Act of 1773. Reorganised judiciary; founded Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784, with Sir William Jones); patronised Sanskrit + Persian studies. Famous trial in Britain (1787-95, acquitted) — accused of corruption + atrocities (Pitt's Bill). LORD CORNWALLIS (1786-93) — Permanent Settlement of Bengal (1793). LORD WELLESLEY (1798-1805) — Subsidiary Alliance system; defeated Tipu (1799). LORD DALHOUSIE (1848-56) — Doctrine of Lapse; first railway 1853.

questions.stem: The PERMANENT SETTLEMENT (Zamindari system) of Bengal in 1793 was introduced by:

options.option_text: Warren Hastings, the first Governor-General
Lord Cornwallis, the Governor-General then
Lord Curzon, much later in the early 1900s
Lord Mountbatten, the last Viceroy of India

questions.explanation: Permanent Settlement of Bengal — introduced by LORD CORNWALLIS in 1793. Made zamindars (intermediaries) the legal owners of land in exchange for fixed revenue (~9/10 to British, 1/10 to zamindar). Long-term consequences: rural impoverishment, rise of absentee landlordism, fall of village community. Other Cornwallis reforms: separated revenue + judicial administration; introduced civil service exams. Distractor 3 — Curzon partitioned Bengal (1905). Distractor 4 — Mountbatten oversaw partition (1947).

questions.stem: The DOCTRINE OF LAPSE — annexing princely states without male heirs — was associated with:

options.option_text: Lord Dalhousie, Governor-General 1848-1856
Lord William Bentinck, the abolitionist of sati
Lord Curzon, who partitioned Bengal in 1905
Lord Hardinge, of the second Sikh war fame

questions.explanation: Doctrine of Lapse — Lord Dalhousie (1848-56). If a ruler died without a NATURAL male heir, the state would 'lapse' to the Company. Annexed: Satara (1848), Jaipur + Sambalpur (1849), Udaipur (1852), Jhansi (1853 — leading to 1857 revolt by Rani Lakshmibai), Nagpur (1854), Awadh (1856 — annexed on 'misrule' grounds, not lapse). Also abolished titles + pensions of ex-Mughal/Maratha figures (Nana Sahib's grievance). Major contributor to 1857 anger. Lord Canning (1856-62) repudiated the doctrine after the revolt.

questions.stem: The PARTITION OF BENGAL (1905), which sparked nationalist protests, was decreed by:

options.option_text: Lord Curzon, Viceroy of India 1899-1905
Lord Hardinge, Viceroy of India 1910-1916
Lord Dalhousie, Governor-General 1848-56
Lord Wellesley, Governor-General 1798-1805

questions.explanation: Lord Curzon (1899-1905) — partitioned Bengal (October 1905) along religious lines, ostensibly for administrative efficiency, actually to weaken Bengali nationalism. Sparked SWADESHI Movement, boycott of British goods. Annulled in 1911 by Lord Hardinge — and capital shifted from Calcutta to DELHI same year. Curzon's other acts: Universities Act (1904), founded Archaeological Survey reforms, Younghusband expedition to Tibet (1903-04). Resigned 1905 over conflict with C-in-C Kitchener.

questions.stem: Sati was officially ABOLISHED in British India in 1829 under the Governor-General:

options.option_text: Lord William Bentinck, with Raja Rammohun Roy's support
Lord Cornwallis, of Permanent Settlement fame
Lord Wellesley, the architect of subsidiary alliance
Lord Auckland, of the First Anglo-Afghan War

questions.explanation: Lord William Bentinck (1828-1835) — Governor-General of India. ABOLISHED SATI by Regulation XVII of December 1829 (Bengal Presidency; extended to other regions later). Strongly supported by RAJA RAMMOHUN ROY (founder of Brahmo Samaj, 1828). Other Bentinck reforms: suppressed Thuggee (Col. Sleeman); promoted ENGLISH-MEDIUM education following Macaulay's Minute (1835); ended ritual female infanticide. Often called 'the most liberal' of British governors.

questions.stem: The FIRST RAILWAY LINE in India (Bombay to Thane, ~34 km) was opened in 1853 under:

options.option_text: Lord Dalhousie, Governor-General 1848-1856
Lord Curzon, Viceroy 1899 to 1905
Lord Canning, Viceroy 1858 to 1862
Lord Mountbatten, last Viceroy in 1947

questions.explanation: First Indian railway: Bombay (Bori Bunder) → Thane, opened 16 April 1853, 34 km, under Lord DALHOUSIE. He saw railways as integral to colonial control + commerce. By his retirement (1856), 200+ miles of rail laid + plans for thousands more. Other Dalhousie 'firsts': telegraph (1851, Calcutta-Diamond Harbour), uniform postage stamp (1854), first electric telegraph from Calcutta to Agra (1854). Ranks among the most consequential British rulers in India in infrastructure terms.

questions.stem: The LAST VICEROY of British India was:

options.option_text: Lord Wavell, Viceroy from 1943 to 1947 March
Lord Mountbatten, Viceroy from March to August 1947
C. Rajagopalachari, the first Indian Governor-General
Lord Linlithgow, Viceroy from 1936 to 1943

questions.explanation: Lord Mountbatten (Louis Francis Mountbatten) — last VICEROY of British India (24 March - 15 August 1947) AND first Governor-General of independent India (Aug 1947 - June 1948). Husband of Edwina Mountbatten. Oversaw partition + transfer of power. 3 June 1947 plan = his blueprint. After his return to UK, C. RAJAGOPALACHARI became the 1st Indian + LAST Governor-General of India (June 1948 - Jan 1950, when India became Republic and post abolished). Wavell preceded Mountbatten; Linlithgow earlier.
